paragraphs: Remember the "password expires in 24 hours" email Jordan Pike forwarded last night? Jordan came in this afternoon and admitted clicking the link before forwarding it, and typing their password into the page.
IT reset the password at 4:50 PM. But the dispatch reporting server, kl-rpt-01, takes the same company login, and it's reachable from outside. Find out whether anyone used Jordan's account there.
You have a read-only forensic session. The server is evidence: nothing you type can change it. Your case notes are in your home folder.
Every command you run takes time. Fill out the case file before 6 AM, when it goes to the day crew as is.

Opened by: R. Vance, SOC Manager
You have a read-only forensic session on kl-rpt-01. Nothing you type can
change the server, so look anywhere you like.
Jordan Pike typed their password into a phishing page early Friday, Nov 27.
IT reset it at 4:50 PM Friday. Find out if anyone used it on this server
before then, and what they left behind.
1. The account the attacker logged in with
2. The IP address they came from
4. How they plan to get back in
5. Where they staged data to steal
Where I'd start: the system logs are in /var/log. Type help for commands.
Files whose names start with a dot are hidden from a plain ls.
For this case the forensic account can read system folders that real servers
usually keep root-only, such as /var/spool/cron (every user's crontab).
working from home: connect the VPN first (you get a 10.40.x address)
IT says if the VPN is down, this box takes logins from outside too
Thanksgiving: covering 2 to 5 PM for Maria
ask Sam for October route utilization numbers
- November fuel card audit to Finance by Monday (copy of fuel_card_usage.csv is in my home folder)
- Thanksgiving coverage: Jordan has 2 to 5 PM

clues.label: Found the attacker's successful login in auth.log
Read the attacker's commands in jpike's hidden shell history
Found the hidden staging folder in /tmp

caseFile.label: Compromised account
caseFile.prompt: Which account did the attacker log in with?
caseFile.help: The username on kl-rpt-01, exactly as the server's logs show it.
caseFile.evidence: /var/log/auth.log: "Accepted password for jpike from 203.0.113.47" at Nov 27 03:14:22. /etc/passwd maps jpike to Jordan Pike.
caseFile.explanation: The attacker logged in as jpike, Jordan's account, with the password Jordan typed into the phishing page about three hours earlier. Nobody had to break anything: a stolen, valid login is all it took.

caseFile.label: Attacker IP address
caseFile.prompt: What IP address did the attacker connect from?
caseFile.help: The address the successful malicious login came from.
caseFile.evidence: /var/log/auth.log and last: jpike from 203.0.113.47 on Fri Nov 27, 03:14 to 03:41. The same address appears in the persistence script.
caseFile.explanation: 203.0.113.47 is the only outside address that got in. 198.51.100.23 made over 200 noisy attempts but never succeeded, and 10.40.12.88 is Jordan's normal VPN address. Loud doesn't mean successful: always look for the Accepted line.

caseFile.label: Attacker commands
caseFile.prompt: Which of these did the attacker do? Check every one, and only those.
caseFile.help: Shell history records commands in the order they were typed.

options.text: Created a new user account with useradd
Copied an archive off the server with scp
Bundled files into an archive with tar
Deleted the system logs with rm -rf /var/log
Added an entry to their crontab

caseFile.evidence: /home/jpike/.bash_history (a hidden file): everything after Jordan's own "exit", from whoami to the second exit. auth.log confirms the failed sudo at 03:16:48.
caseFile.explanation: The attacker looked around (whoami, id, uname), tried and failed to become root, copied the customer and driver exports into a hidden folder, bundled them with tar, downloaded a script from their own server with curl, and scheduled it with cron. They never created a user, never deleted logs, and haven't sent the archive anywhere yet: it's still sitting in /tmp.

caseFile.label: Persistence
caseFile.prompt: How does the attacker keep access after the password reset?
caseFile.help: Persistence is anything that lets an attacker back in, or keeps their code running, after the original way in is closed.
caseFile.pathLabel: Full path of the file it runs
caseFile.evidence: /var/spool/cron/crontabs/jpike runs /home/jpike/.local/share/.sysd-update.sh every 15 minutes. /var/log/syslog shows it running all day, long after the 4:50 PM reset, and ps shows it running now.
caseFile.explanation: A cron job runs the hidden script every 15 minutes as jpike. The script checks in with 203.0.113.47 and runs whatever comes back. Resetting the password closed the front door, but this was already inside. To clean up: remove the crontab entry and the script, then check for anything it pulled down.

caseFile.label: Data staged for theft
caseFile.prompt: Where did the attacker stage the data they plan to steal?
caseFile.help: Staged data is copied and packed up, ready to send out. Give the full path.
caseFile.evidence: ls -la /tmp shows the hidden folder .cache-x (owned by jpike) holding sys-update.tgz, created Nov 27 03:33. The shell history shows what went into it.
caseFile.explanation: The attacker packed customers_2026Q4.csv and driver_roster.csv into /tmp/.cache-x/sys-update.tgz. The dot hides the folder from a plain ls, and the harmless-sounding name is camouflage. The originals in /srv/dispatch/exports are where the data came from, not where it was staged.

timeline.text: The phishing email "Your password expires in 24 hours" arrives from kestre1-logistics.com (a 1 in place of the l).
Jordan clicks the link, types their password into verify-acct.net, and only then forwards the email to the SOC.
One failed try, then a successful SSH login as jpike from 203.0.113.47.
The attacker looks around: whoami, id, uname -a.
Tries sudo cat /etc/shadow to grab every password hash on the server. Refused: jpike isn't a sudoer.
Copies customers_2026Q4.csv and driver_roster.csv into the hidden folder /tmp/.cache-x, packs them into sys-update.tgz, and deletes the loose copies.
Downloads .sysd-update.sh from 203.0.113.47 with curl into a hidden folder and makes it executable.
Adds a crontab entry that runs the script every 15 minutes.
Logs out after 27 minutes on the server.
Cron starts the script every 15 minutes. It checks in with 203.0.113.47 and runs whatever comes back.
IT resets Jordan's password. The cron job keeps running anyway: a password reset doesn't remove persistence.
You connect. The script is still running as jpike, and the archive is still sitting in /tmp.

audit.title: Why the attacker's commands were still on disk
audit.text: Kestrel's shell audit policy, /etc/profile.d/kestrel-audit.sh, sets PROMPT_COMMAND='history -a', so bash writes each command to ~/.bash_history the moment it runs instead of at logout. A dropped connection, or clearing the shell's in-memory history, can't erase what's already been written. Without that policy, this case would have had a lot less to go on.
audit.seen: You read the policy during the shift.
audit.unseen: You didn't open it tonight. It's worth a look: cat /etc/profile.d/kestrel-audit.sh

recommendations: Remove the persistence: delete jpike's crontab entry and /home/jpike/.local/share/.sysd-update.sh, stop the running script (PID 3431), and check for anything it downloaded.
Block 203.0.113.47 at the firewall and search every other server's logs for it.
Keep /tmp/.cache-x/sys-update.tgz as evidence, and treat the customer and driver data as exposed until the network logs prove otherwise.
Require multifactor authentication for remote logins, so a stolen password alone isn't enough to get in.
Only allow SSH to kl-rpt-01 over the VPN, never straight from the internet.
Report a click right away, even after forwarding the email. The attacker was in three hours after Jordan's click; the reset came thirteen hours after that.
debrief.nextNight: Open question for tomorrow night: the archive is packed, but the attacker never ran scp or anything else to send it. The script phones home every 15 minutes, though, and runs whatever it's told. Did anything leave? That's a job for the network logs.
